title: We All Need To Be Constrained
author: The Daily Stoic
summary: This short Daily Stoic entry attacks the flattering assumption that power would leave us unchanged. Its argument runs through Marcus Aurelius, who is treated not as proof that good character survives the throne but as the rare exception whose own journals record him fighting off corruption. If the best emperor in history needed to write himself warnings about being stained purple, the piece argues, the rest of us should stop imagining we are immune. From there it turns practical, listing the external constraints a person needs: partners who tell the truth, collaborators who offset weaknesses, a board that surfaces conflicts of interest, and philosophy itself as a standing review of one's impulses. The closing move reframes constraint as something other than deprivation. Limits are cast as the conditions of sanity, decency and greatness rather than obstacles to them.
points: The piece inverts the usual reading of Marcus Aurelius, treating his self correction as evidence that power corrupts rather than as evidence that character protects.
It argues that the belief that one would personally be unaffected by wealth, fame or authority is exactly the belief that makes a person dangerous.
The prescribed remedy is structural rather than internal: truthful partners, complementary collaborators and an advisory board that can name conflicts of interest.
Philosophy is positioned as a governance mechanism, a standing review process for one's own impulses rather than a body of doctrine.
Constraint is reframed as productive, with limits presented as what keeps a leader sane and decent instead of as what holds them back.
quotes: We'd like to think we'd do fine if we were ever put in that position. If we were ever given real power, real wealth, real fame, it wouldn't change us, right?
It's just that Marcus Aurelius was so exceptional, he didn't change as much as most everyone else who was emperor. He is, as we have said, the exception that proves the rule.
Well, for starters, no one should be king. More practically, we all need checks and balances in our lives. We need partners who tell us the truth.
We need collaborators who balance out our weaknesses. We need a board of directors who gives us advice and helps us resolve conflicts of interest.
We need philosophy, as Marcus Aurelius used it, to put ourselves up for review and to challenge our impulses.
We should not get to do everything we want. We should not be surrounded by "yes" men and women. We should not think we are superior to others or exempt from constraints.
We need those constraints. They keep us sane. They keep us decent. They make us great.
